title: The behavior of red foxes
body: Red foxes are solitary hunters for most of the year. They pounce on mice hidden under snow, cache extra food, and use more than twenty different calls to talk to each other. In spring the family stays together while the young learn to hunt.

title: Vulpes vulpes: a field guide
body: Vulpes vulpes has the widest range of any wild carnivore, from the Arctic to North Africa. Look for the white-tipped tail, black legs and narrow muzzle. It adapts to farmland, forest edges and even city centres.

title: Fox kits playing outside the den
body: By late April, young foxes start leaving the den to play. They wrestle, chase and practise pouncing while a parent watches nearby. Keep your distance: a disturbed vixen may move the whole litter.

title: How gray wolf packs hunt in winter
body: In deep snow, a wolf pack travels single file to save energy. They test a herd for weak animals and work together to bring down prey many times their size. A pack can cover fifty kilometres in a night.

title: Canis lupus in Yellowstone, thirty years on
body: Canis lupus was reintroduced to Yellowstone in 1995 after seventy years of absence. Researchers have since tracked how the packs changed elk behaviour, river banks and even the number of songbirds.

title: Five tips for training your dog
body: Keep sessions short, reward the behaviour you want within two seconds, and practise in a quiet room before a busy park. Consistency matters more than any trick: everyone in the house should use the same words.

title: Choosing a family dog breed
body: A family dog should match your energy level and space. Retrievers are patient with children, herding breeds need daily work, and small breeds can suit apartments. Visit a shelter before you decide.

title: Grizzly bears waking from hibernation
body: When grizzlies leave their dens in spring, they have lost up to a third of their body weight. They roam open sagebrush and meadows looking for carcasses, roots and new grass, and they are easily surprised.

title: Ursus arctos horribilis on the sagebrush steppe
body: Ursus arctos horribilis can weigh over 300 kilograms and runs faster than a horse over short distances. Its hump is a mass of muscle used for digging. Give it at least a hundred metres of space.

title: Mule deer migration corridors
body: Every autumn, mule deer walk up to 240 kilometres from summer range to winter range. Highways and fences cut these old routes, and wildlife crossings are helping herds get through safely.

title: Why deer grow antlers every year
body: Bucks grow a new set of antlers each summer, covered in velvet that feeds the bone underneath. By autumn the velvet is rubbed off for the rut, and the antlers drop again in late winter.

title: Coyotes are thriving in our cities
body: Coyotes now live in almost every large North American city. They hunt rodents in parks and along rail lines, mostly at night, and they rarely cause trouble if people do not feed them.

title: Wild fox species of North America
body: From the tiny swift fox of the plains to the gray fox that can climb trees, North America has several wild fox species. The most widespread is still the familiar orange one with the white-tipped tail.

title: Keeping indoor cats happy
body: Indoor cats need places to climb, scratch and hide. Short play sessions with a wand toy mimic hunting, and puzzle feeders slow down fast eaters. Rotate toys weekly so they stay interesting.

title: How octopuses use camouflage
body: An octopus can change the colour and texture of its skin in a fraction of a second, matching rock, coral or sand. It does this with thousands of pigment cells controlled directly by its nerves.

title: Baking sourdough bread at home
body: A sourdough starter is just flour, water and time. Feed it daily for a week, then mix the dough, fold it every half hour, and bake in a very hot covered pot for a crackling crust.
